title: One Goddess, nine forms
hook: nine nights, nine forms, and a battlefield where the Goddess says there's no one else
carry: ekam sat: one truth, many names

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ganesha and the laughing moon. Your line was the lord of obstacles humbles pride.

Near the shrine in a North Indian home during Navaratri, you may find a small calendar taped up: one name for each night, all the way to nine. Some families wear a different color each day to match. It looks like nine goddesses. Ask the grandmother who keeps the calendar, and she'll likely tell you: it's one Goddess, nine ways.
screen: `A CALENDAR BY THE SHRINE.` → `ONE NAME FOR EACH NIGHT.` → `ONE GODDESS, NINE WAYS.`

segments.voice: The nine forms are the Navadurga, nine Durgas, and in the common list they move through a life: Shailaputri, daughter of the mountain; Brahmacharini, the seeker who fasts in the forest to win Shiva; Chandraghanta and Kushmanda; Skandamata, the mother; Katyayani, the warrior; Kalaratri, the dark night who destroys fear; Mahagauri, radiant and calm; and Siddhidatri, giver of every attainment. Devotees honor one each night, and many fast. So are they nine goddesses? The Devi Mahatmya, the scripture many read aloud through Navaratri, answers with a story. The demon king Shumbha has watched a whole army of goddesses fight beside Durga. Furious, he taunts her: you're proud, but you only win by leaning on other women's strength. And the Goddess answers: I am alone here in the world. Who else is there besides me? These are my own powers, coming back into me. And every goddess on the field disappears into her body, until she stands alone and faces him herself. That's one of Hinduism's oldest and biggest teachings, and the answer to anyone who asks if Hindus have nine goddesses, or a thousand gods. The Rig Veda says it in four words: ekam sat vipra bahudha vadanti. Truth is one; the wise call it by many names. Many forms, one reality. And on the eighth or ninth day, many families invite young girls home, wash their feet, feed them and honor them as the Goddess: one more form she takes.
screen: `NAVADURGA: NINE FORMS.` · `DAUGHTER, SEEKER, MOTHER, WARRIOR, DARK NIGHT, PEACE.` · `WHO ELSE IS THERE BESIDES ME?` · `EVERY GODDESS RETURNS TO HER.` · then, large: `EKAM SAT: ONE TRUTH, MANY NAMES.`

segments.voice: Many families honor one form of the Goddess each night. Pick the one that fits your week: the seeker who doesn't give up, the mother, the warrior, or the dark night who destroys fear. Say her name softly on a few breaths out, then let it rest into one word: Ma, mother. If you don't pray, name the strength you need, then notice it's the same strength under every name.
Navaratri. Nine nights, nine forms, the Navadurga, and one Goddess under every name.
Your line: ekam sat, one truth, many names. Durga said it on the battlefield: who else is there besides me? Day six hundred seventy-nine, done.

howItsDone: Many Hindus honor one of the nine forms of Durga, the Navadurga, on each night of Navaratri, with that form's prayers and offerings; some fast all nine days, some wear a set color each day, and many end by honoring young girls as the Goddess on the eighth or ninth day.

what a scholar hears: the common list of the Navadurga is often traced to the Devi Kavacham recited with the Devi Mahatmya; the Goddess's 'who else is there besides me?' is Devi Mahatmya 10.5, and 'ekaṃ sad viprā bahudhā vadanti' is Rig Veda 1.164.46.
